title: Very good (Genesis 1:31)
hook: God made the world freely, out of goodness

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trinity: one God, a communion of love from all eternity. Your line was love is a communion. Where did you feel real togetherness? Today, that love spills over into a world. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Think of the last time you made something just because you wanted to. A meal for friends. A drawing for a kid. A garden bed nobody asked for. You didn't need it. You weren't paid. You made it because something in you was full, and it wanted to spill over. And when it was done, you stepped back and looked at it, and something in you said: good. The Bible's first chapter ends with God doing exactly that. Today: creation.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU MADE FOR NO REASON.` → `FULL, AND SPILLING OVER.` → `STEPPING BACK: GOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain. Genesis opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." Then, day after day, as light and sea and plants and animals appear, the same line comes back: God saw that it was good. And at the end, after human beings are made: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." In Hebrew, tov me'od. Not just good. Very good. Second, why God made it. The Catechism says God didn't create because he needed anything, or was lonely, or bored. God created freely, out of wisdom and goodness, to share his own goodness. Remember yesterday: God was never alone. So creation isn't God filling a gap. It's love spilling over. Third, out of nothing. Catholics believe God created not from some material already lying around, but from nothing at all. Everything that exists, from galaxies to the dust on your windowsill, exists because God wants it to, right now. And here's a surprise: the Catechism says the six days are presented symbolically, a picture of God's work, not a stopwatch. Catholics are free to learn from science how the world developed. Fourth, what very good means for a Tuesday. The Catechism says each creature has its own particular goodness, reflecting something of God. Saint Francis of Assisi sang to Brother Sun and Sister Moon. Pope Francis took his 2015 letter on the environment, Laudato Si', from that song. A world God called very good is worth noticing, thanking, and caring for.
screen: `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.` · `NOT NEEDED, BUT SHARED.` · `OUT OF NOTHING, BY LOVE.` · `EACH CREATURE ITS OWN GOODNESS.` · then, large: `IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one thing in nature. Look for something alive or natural near you: a plant on the sill, a tree through the window, the sky, a dog asleep, even your own breath. Look at it as God's handiwork, made on purpose, wanted into being. Let yourself say, inside: very good. If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did. If not, simply be glad it exists. The bell holds the time.
Creation. Everything God made freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness: and he called it very good. Today's word.
Your line: it was very good. Today, step outside for one minute, look at one living thing, and say it under your breath: very good. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at every Sunday Mass, bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis on October 4, and many now keep a Season of Creation each September.

fork.setup: God has finished making the world, including human beings. God steps back and looks. what's the verdict?
fork.reveal: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." only after humans appear does good become very good.

original.note: Hebrew: very good, God's verdict on everything at the end of the sixth day.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation is a story about how long it took.
what it means: God made the world freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness, and called it very good.
what a scholar hears: tov me'od; creatio ex nihilo (2 Maccabees 7:28); CCC 295–301 and 337–339; and Francis's Canticle of the Creatures behind Laudato Si'.
